title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Hyperscale Data ditches Bitcoin mining for AI in Cass County—what it means for power and towns.

lines.text: Good morning, and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Today we're talking about a big shift at a Cass County site where Bitcoin mining is shutting down to make room for AI operations.
That sounds like a sign of where things are heading with these facilities.
Exactly. Hyperscale Data is halting all its miners effective September 1 at the Michigan site.
Why make the change now?
They're moving under a master services agreement projected to generate $1.2 billion, with expansion options that could reach $3 billion.
That's serious money. How much of the facility are we talking about?
Up to 20 percent of the site's 340 megawatt capacity.
So they're not using the whole thing for AI right away?
Not yet, but the deal leaves room to grow.
What does this tell us about the broader trend in Michigan?
It shows how some operators are repurposing existing infrastructure as demand for AI computing rises.
Crypto mining used a lot of power too, right?
Yes, but AI workloads can be even more intensive depending on the setup.
How might this affect local electric bills in Cass County?
The facility already draws significant load, so any expansion could factor into future rate cases for the utility serving the area.
What about water use for cooling?
Data centers in general need substantial water, and rural spots like Cass County often rely on local sources.
Is farmland involved here?
Many of these sites go up on former agricultural land, which raises questions about long-term land use.
Who are the main players in this deal?
Hyperscale Data is the operator, and they're signing with a customer under that master services agreement.
What happens next at the site?
They'll start ramping up AI operations while keeping options open for more capacity.
Could this model spread to other Michigan locations?
It's possible if more crypto sites find AI customers willing to pay premium rates.
How does this fit with all the local pushback we're seeing elsewhere?
It highlights the tension between economic deals and community concerns over infrastructure strain.
Residents in places like Decatur are already clashing over similar proposals.
Yes, yesterday they debated property taxes, noise, and grid impacts.
Supporters mention jobs, but opponents worry about higher bills.
That's the core tradeoff playing out in small towns across the state.
Meanwhile, Rep. James is arguing for more local control over rules.
He says cities and townships should decide for themselves, even though his past votes leaned the other way.
That shift could change how projects get approved.
It would give communities more say on zoning and incentives.
Senator Runestad wants to end sales-tax breaks for new centers.
Yesterday he pushed to repeal those exemptions so projects pay more into state coffers.
That could mean more revenue but also higher costs passed along.
Lawmakers will have to weigh that against job and investment arguments.
Consumers Energy is already doing grid work in West Michigan.
Yes, yesterday they started Cherry Street upgrades tied to rising demand from data centers and other big users.
Will customers see rate impacts from that?
Eventually yes, as the utility recovers those costs.
Detroit residents are facing blackout risks too.
Yesterday groups called for a freeze on new projects while the city writes power and water rules.
A moratorium would buy time to assess the strain.
Mike Rogers is calling for a statewide pause until utilities prove they can handle the load.
He wants no new approvals if bills would go up for residents.
Voters from both parties have raised the same concern.
Ypsilanti is debating its own year-long halt tonight.
City leaders will consider a temporary ban on standalone proposals.
Residents there fear spikes in rates and water use.
A moratorium would let them craft permanent zoning first.
Vance tied data centers to power bills and jobs during his Sterling Heights stop yesterday.
He framed the growth as both opportunity and risk for household costs.
Closed-door pitches are also raising eyebrows.
Yesterday officials heard presentations while demonstrators rallied outside.
Residents miles away could still feel the effects on bills and water.
The format left some wondering whose voices count most in these deals.
So what's on deck for listeners who want to weigh in?
Ypsilanti's city council meets tonight to debate that year-long pause on new data centers.
That sounds like a key one for residents worried about rates and water.
Decatur's ongoing clash over the proposed campus is another one to watch.
Those debates are shaping up as test cases for other small towns.
We'll keep tracking how these local fights connect to the bigger grid picture.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Michigan Data Wire: Cass County AI Pivot and Statewide Data Center Tensions
